\chapter{Overview}
\label{\detokenize{Overview:overview}}\label{\detokenize{Overview::doc}}

\section{DynamiSpectra: from molecular dynamics simulations to comprehensive data analysis}
\label{\detokenize{Overview:dynamispectra-from-molecular-dynamics-simulations-to-comprehensive-data-analysis}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} is an advanced Python package designed for analyzing molecular dynamics simulation data. Built to process and interpret results primarily from \sphinxtitleref{GROMACS https://www.gromacs.org/} structure, \sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} provides a streamlined and efficient workflow for researchers in the field of molecular dynamics. By leveraging the power of Python, this package enables users to perform complex analyses, visualize molecular behaviors, and gain valuable insights from simulation outputs. Whether you’re studying protein folding, ligand interactions, or other molecular phenomena, \sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} empowers you to dive deep into your data and uncover meaningful patterns.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It provides powerful tools to calculate and visualize a wide range of molecular properties, including Hydrogen bonds, Root Mean Square Deviation, Root Mean Square Fluctuation, Solvent Accessible Surface Area, Radius of Gyration, Secondary Structure Analysis, and Principal component. These features enable researchers to gain deep insights into the dynamics of molecular systems, study conformational changes, and investigate interactions between molecules with greater precision.


\section{Installation}
\label{\detokenize{Overview:installation}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{pip} \PYG{n}{install} \PYG{n}{DynamiSpectra}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can also install the in\sphinxhyphen{}development version with:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{pip} \PYG{n}{install} \PYG{n}{https}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{github}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{com}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{Conradoou}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{DynamiSpectra}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{archive}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{main}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{zip}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note: \sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} uses the package SciPy, which requires a fortran compiler to be installed to build its source,which can be tricky on some systems. An alternative to this is to use Anaconda environment. \sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} can then be more easily installed within this environment, using the command line or preferred method. Installing \sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} may take some time on certain systems. If you observe the command line halting, please be patient, as the installation process may require seconds to minutes to complete.

\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} provides a variety of data analysis tools for GROMACS output files:


\section{Root Mean Square Deviation}
\label{\detokenize{Input:root-mean-square-deviation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} requires GROMACS output files with the \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} extension for RMSD analysis. These files must contain the time series of atomic deviations during the simulation, typically generated using the \sphinxtitleref{gmx rms} tool from GROMACS. The \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} file is expected to have two columns: the first representing simulation time in nanoseconds (ns), and the second containing RMSD values in nanometers (nm). These values correspond to the deviation of the selected atoms or groups of atoms over time, in relation to a reference structure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To generate this file using GROMACS, the following command can be used:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }rms\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}o\PYG{+w}{ }rmsd.xvg\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}tu\PYG{+w}{ }ns
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} allows the analysis of one or more simulation groups. Each group can include one or multiple replicate \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} files. The analysis function automatically computes the average and standard deviation across replicates for each group and produces both time\sphinxhyphen{}resolved and density plots.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Code Execution}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The analysis is performed by calling the \sphinxtitleref{rmsd\_analysis} function from the RMSD module:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{dynamispectra}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{RMSD}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{rmsd\PYGZus{}analysis}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Run the analysis}
\PYG{n}{rmsd\PYGZus{}analysis}\PYG{p}{(}
    \PYG{n}{output\PYGZus{}folder}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{simulation1\PYGZus{}files}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{simulation2\PYGZus{}files}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{simulation3\PYGZus{}files}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{rmsd\PYGZus{}config}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{rmsd\PYGZus{}config}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{density\PYGZus{}config}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{density\PYGZus{}config}
\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxtitleref{rmsd\_config} and \sphinxtitleref{density\_config} dictionaries allow users to customize the appearance of the plots. All fields are optional, and default values will be applied if no configuration is provided.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Although the function supports multiple groups with replicates, it also works with a single group and a single replicate. For example, calling:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{rmsd\PYGZus{}analysis}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{output\PYGZus{}folder}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{simulation1\PYGZus{}files}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
is sufficient to generate RMSD and density plots for just one simulation set. This flexibility allows users to perform both basic and comparative analyses without modifying the source code, regardless of the number of replicates available.


\section{Root Mean Square Fluctuation}
\label{\detokenize{Input:root-mean-square-fluctuation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} requires GROMACS output files with the \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} extension for RMSF analysis. These files must contain the root mean square fluctuation of each residue, typically generated using the \sphinxtitleref{gmx rmsf} tool from GROMACS. The \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} file must contain two columns: the first indicating the residue number, and the second representing the RMSF value (nm) for each residue. These values quantify the flexibility or mobility of each residue along the simulation trajectory.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To generate the required file using GROMACS, the following command can be used:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }rmsf\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}o\PYG{+w}{ }rmsf.xvg\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}res
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} allows analyzing one or more simulation groups, each optionally containing multiple replicate \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} files. The analysis function computes the average and standard deviation across replicates and generates two types of plots: a per\sphinxhyphen{}residue fluctuation curve and a density distribution of RMSF values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Code Execution}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Import the analysis function:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{dynamispectra}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{RMSF}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{rmsf\PYGZus{}analysis}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\sphinxAtStartPar
Both configuration dictionaries (\sphinxtitleref{rmsf\_config} and \sphinxtitleref{density\_config}) are optional. If not provided, the function will generate plots with default layout and colors. This flexibility allows users to customize plots according to their preferences while keeping the function compatible with both simple and advanced use cases.


\section{Radius of Gyration}
\label{\detokenize{Input:radius-of-gyration}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} requires GROMACS output files with the \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} extension for Radius of Gyration (Rg) analysis. These files should contain the time series of Rg values computed during the simulation, typically generated with the \sphinxtitleref{gmx gyrate} tool. The \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} file must include the simulation time in nanoseconds (ns) in the first column and the total radius of gyration in nanometers (nm) in the second column. Additional columns (typically third to fifth) may include component values along the X, Y, and Z axes, though only the total Rg (second column) is used in this analysis.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To generate a compatible file using GROMACS, the following command can be used:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }gyrate\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}o\PYG{+w}{ }gyrate.xvg
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The analysis supports one or more simulation groups, each potentially composed of multiple replicate \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} files. \sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} calculates average and standard deviation across replicates for each group, and produces both a time\sphinxhyphen{}resolved plot and a distribution (KDE) plot of the Rg values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Code Execution}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Import the analysis function from the Rg module:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{dynamispectra}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{Rg}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{rg\PYGZus{}analysis}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is also possible to run the analysis using a single group with only one replicate. For example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{rg\PYGZus{}analysis}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{output\PYGZus{}folder}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{simulation1\PYGZus{}files}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
All plot configuration dictionaries are optional. If omitted, the plots will be generated with default visual settings. This design allows users to tailor the visualization for presentations or publications without altering the analysis logic.


\section{Hydrogen Bond Analysis}
\label{\detokenize{Input:hydrogen-bond-analysis}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} requires \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} output files from GROMACS for hydrogen bond analysis. These files are typically generated using the \sphinxtitleref{gmx hbond} tool and must contain the time\sphinxhyphen{}resolved data of H\sphinxhyphen{}bond interactions observed during molecular dynamics simulations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} file must have the following structure:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Column 1: Simulation time in nanoseconds

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Column 2: Total number of hydrogen bonds detected at each time point

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Column 3: Number of atom pairs within 0.35 nm (potential H\sphinxhyphen{}bond candidates)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These data enable detailed tracking of H\sphinxhyphen{}bond dynamics and the compactness or rearrangement of molecular systems throughout the simulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To generate the required \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} file using GROMACS:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }hbond\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}num\PYG{+w}{ }hbond.xvg\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}tu\PYG{+w}{ }ns
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} supports analysis of one or multiple simulation groups, each optionally including several replicate files. It computes the average and standard deviation of H\sphinxhyphen{}bond counts across replicates and generates both time\sphinxhyphen{}resolved and density plots.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Code Execution}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Import the H\sphinxhyphen{}bond analysis function:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{dynamispectra}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{Hbond}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{hbond\PYGZus{}analysis}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

You can also run the analysis with a single group and a single replicate:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If configuration dictionaries are omitted, \sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} will generate the plots with default settings. These customization options allow full control of the appearance for publications or presentations.


\section{Solvent Accessible Surface Area}
\label{\detokenize{Input:solvent-accessible-surface-area}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} requires \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} output files from GROMACS for SASA analysis. These files are typically generated using the \sphinxtitleref{gmx sasa} tool and provide time\sphinxhyphen{}resolved measurements of the solvent\sphinxhyphen{}accessible surface area of the selected atoms during the simulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} file must follow this format:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Column 1: Simulation time (ps)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Column 2: Total SASA (nm²) of the selected group of atoms over time

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This information enables detailed evaluation of conformational changes and solvation properties of the system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To generate the required \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} file using GROMACS:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }sasa\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}o\PYG{+w}{ }sasa.xvg\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}probe\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}.14
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} supports multiple simulation groups, each with one or more replicates. The package automatically aligns time series, computes mean and standard deviation, and generates plots for both time evolution and density distribution of SASA.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Code Execution}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Import the SASA analysis module:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{dynamispectra}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{SASA}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{sasa\PYGZus{}analysis}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

If no configuration dictionaries are provided, default settings will be used. Customize the plots as needed to match the desired presentation style or publication format.


\section{Salt Bridge}
\label{\detokenize{Input:salt-bridge}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} requires \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} output files from GROMACS for salt bridge analysis between the ligand and the protein, or only protein. These files are typically generated using the \sphinxtitleref{gmx mindist} tool with appropriate index groups and contain time series of minimum distances between charged groups.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} file must follow this format:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Column 1: Simulation time (ps)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Column 2: Minimum salt\sphinxhyphen{}bridge distance (nm) between charged groups over time

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This data allows monitoring the presence or absence of salt\sphinxhyphen{}bridge interactions during the simulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To generate the required \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} file using GROMACS:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }mindist\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }index.ndx\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}od\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xvg\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}on\PYG{+w}{ }saltbridge.xvg\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}group\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}d\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}.4
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} supports multiple simulation groups, each with one or more replicates. The package automatically aligns time series, computes mean and standard deviation, and generates plots for both time evolution and density distribution of salt\sphinxhyphen{}bridge distances.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Code Execution}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Import the salt bridge analysis module:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{dynamispectra}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{saltbridge}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{saltbridge\PYGZus{}analysis}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\section{Protein–Ligand Contacts}
\label{\detokenize{Input:proteinligand-contacts}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} requires \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} output files from GROMACS for analyzing the number of atomic contacts between protein and ligand during the simulation. These files are typically generated using the \sphinxtitleref{gmx mindist} or \sphinxtitleref{gmx contact} tool with appropriate index groups for the protein and ligand atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} file must follow this format:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Column 1: Simulation time (ps)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Column 2: Number of contacts between the selected groups over time

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This information allows monitoring interaction stability, binding dynamics, and fluctuation of protein–ligand contacts across time.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To generate the required \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} file using GROMACS:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }mindist\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }index.ndx\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}on\PYG{+w}{ }contacts.xvg\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}d\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}.35
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} supports multiple simulation groups, each with one or more replicates. The package automatically aligns time series, computes mean and standard deviation, and generates plots for both time evolution and density distribution of contacts.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Code Execution}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Import the contact analysis module:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{dynamispectra}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{Contacts}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{contact\PYGZus{}analysis}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} requires \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} output files from GROMACS to analyze the minimum distance between protein and ligand atoms during molecular dynamics simulations. These files are typically generated using the \sphinxtitleref{gmx distance} tool with selected atom groups from an index file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} file must follow this format:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Column 1: Simulation time (ps)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Column 2: Minimum distance (nm) between protein and ligand atoms at each time point

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This analysis allows the evaluation of binding stability, complex dissociation, and proximity of interaction over time.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To generate the required \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} file using GROMACS:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }mindist\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }index.ndx\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}od\PYG{+w}{ }mindist.xvg\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}d\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}.35
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} supports multiple simulation groups, each with one or more replicates. The tool aligns all time series, computes mean and standard deviation, and generates plots showing time evolution and the distribution of distances.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Code Execution}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Import the distance analysis module:

\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\section{Protein\sphinxhyphen{}Ligand Hydrophobic Contacts}
\label{\detokenize{Input:protein-ligand-hydrophobic-contacts}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} supports the analysis of hydrophobic contacts between ligand and protein from \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} files. These files typically represent the number of hydrophobic contacts over time, generated using custom GROMACS selections involving hydrophobic atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} file must follow this format:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Column 1: Simulation time (ps)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Column 2: Number of hydrophobic contacts between ligand and protein

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This analysis helps to evaluate the contribution of nonpolar interactions to the stability and binding of protein–ligand complexes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To generate \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} files, you can use GROMACS with \sphinxtitleref{gmx select} or other post\sphinxhyphen{}processing tools with appropriate selections:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{select}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }index.ndx\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}select\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}group \PYGZdq{}LIG\PYGZdq{} and within 0.6 of group \PYGZdq{}Protein\PYGZdq{}\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}os\PYG{+w}{ }hydrophobic\PYGZus{}contacts.xvg
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\section{Inter\sphinxhyphen{}residue Distance Matrix}
\label{\detokenize{Input:inter-residue-distance-matrix}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} supports the visualization of inter\sphinxhyphen{}residue distance matrices using \sphinxtitleref{.xpm} files generated by GROMACS. These matrices represent the average distances between residue pairs throughout a trajectory and are useful for identifying compact or flexible regions within a protein.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxtitleref{.xpm} file can be generated using the following GROMACS command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }mdmat\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}mean\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xpm\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}no\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xvg
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This analysis is typically used for all\sphinxhyphen{}against\sphinxhyphen{}all residue contact distances in a protein structure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Code Execution}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Import the distance matrix analysis module:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{dynamispectra}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{DistanceMatrix}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{distance\PYGZus{}matrix\PYGZus{}analysis}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\section{Phi and Psi Angles}
\label{\detokenize{Input:phi-and-psi-angles}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} analyzes backbone dihedral angles φ (phi) and ψ (psi) from \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} files generated by GROMACS. These files contain Ramachandran angle distributions used to assess protein conformational states over time.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} files can be generated with the following GROMACS command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }rama\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}o\PYG{+w}{ }rama.xvg
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This analysis creates kernel density estimation (KDE) heatmaps of φ\sphinxhyphen{}ψ angle distributions, helping identify favored secondary structure conformations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Code Execution}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Import the phi\sphinxhyphen{}psi analysis module:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\section{Rotamers (Dihedral χ1 and χ2 Angles)}
\label{\detokenize{Input:rotamers-dihedral-1-and-2-angles}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} supports detailed analysis of side\sphinxhyphen{}chain rotamer states through the dihedral angles χ1 and χ2 extracted from .xvg files generated by GROMACS. This analysis helps characterize conformational changes and rotamer preferences during molecular dynamics simulations. Circular mean statistics are used to average χ1 and χ2 angles across replicates, properly accounting for their periodic nature. This module generates three types of plots to visualize rotamer distributions.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{KDE}: Kernel Density Estimation (2D KDE heatmap) showing the probability density of χ1 and χ2 angles combined.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Dotplot}: Scatter plot filtered by the selected time window.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Histogram (Hist)}: Distribution plots of χ1 and χ2 angles separately, showing frequency density.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can extract χ1 and χ2 dihedral angles with GROMACS using commands like:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }chi\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }index.ndx\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}o\PYG{+w}{ }chi1.xvg\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}type\PYG{+w}{ }dihedral
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }chi\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }index.ndx\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}o\PYG{+w}{ }chi2.xvg\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}type\PYG{+w}{ }dihedral
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These visualizations provide a comprehensive view of side\sphinxhyphen{}chain conformations during the simulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Note:} The atom groups defining the χ1 and χ2 dihedral angles must be correctly specified in the GROMACS index file (\sphinxtitleref{.ndx}) prior to angle calculation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Code Execution}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\end{sphinxVerbatim}

    \PYG{l+s+sa}{r}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{E:}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Conrado}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{PNU}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Dynamics}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{rotamers\PYGZus{}chi1\PYGZus{}chi2}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{chi1\PYGZus{}time\PYGZus{}Rep2.xvg}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{l+s+sa}{r}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{E:}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Conrado}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{PNU}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Dynamics}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{rotamers\PYGZus{}chi1\PYGZus{}chi2}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{chi1\PYGZus{}time\PYGZus{}Rep3.xvg}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}

    \PYG{l+s+sa}{r}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{E:}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Conrado}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{PNU}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Dynamics}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{rotamers\PYGZus{}chi1\PYGZus{}chi2}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{chi2\PYGZus{}time\PYGZus{}Rep2.xvg}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{l+s+sa}{r}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{E:}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Conrado}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{PNU}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Dynamics}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{rotamers\PYGZus{}chi1\PYGZus{}chi2}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{chi2\PYGZus{}time\PYGZus{}Rep3.xvg}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}

\section{Ligand Density}
\label{\detokenize{Input:ligand-density}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} enables visualization of ligand density maps using \sphinxtitleref{.xpm} files generated by GROMACS. These maps represent the spatial occupancy of ligand atoms around the target molecule during the simulation, helping identify preferred binding regions or solvent\sphinxhyphen{}exposed areas.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxtitleref{.xpm} file can be generated with a GROMACS command such as:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }densmap\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }index.ndx\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}o\PYG{+w}{ }ligand\PYGZus{}density.xpm
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This analysis provides a 2D heatmap of ligand occupancy, with colors representing the frequency of ligand presence in specific spatial bins.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Code Execution}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Import the ligand density analysis module:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{dynamispectra}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{ligand\PYGZus{}density}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{ligand\PYGZus{}density\PYGZus{}analysis}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Example usage for one \sphinxtitleref{.xpm} file and specifying output plot parameters:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\sphinxAtStartPar
The resulting plots are saved in \sphinxtitleref{.png} and \sphinxtitleref{.tiff} formats at the specified output location.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To use default plotting parameters, call the function with just the \sphinxtitleref{.xpm} file and output path:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{ligand\PYGZus{}density\PYGZus{}analysis}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{xpm\PYGZus{}file\PYGZus{}path}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{output\PYGZus{}path}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\section{Ligand Dihedral Angle Analysis}
\label{\detokenize{Input:ligand-dihedral-angle-analysis}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} provides analysis and visualization of ligand dihedral angles over time, allowing insight into conformational changes and flexibility of ligand torsions during molecular dynamics simulations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Input data consist of \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} files containing dihedral angle values measured at each simulation frame for multiple replicas across different simulation groups.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }gangle\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.ndx\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}g1\PYG{+w}{ }dihedral\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}group1\PYG{+w}{ }diedro\PYGZus{}1\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}oall\PYG{+w}{ }diedro\PYGZus{}ligand.xvg
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Note:} To extract ligand dihedral angles using GROMACS, the specific atoms defining each dihedral must be pre\sphinxhyphen{}defined in the index (\sphinxtitleref{.ndx}) file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Code Execution}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Import the ligand angle analysis function:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\section{Principal Component Analysis (PCA)}
\label{\detokenize{Input:principal-component-analysis-pca}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} provides tools to visualize and interpret the results of principal component analysis (PCA) applied to molecular dynamics trajectories. This analysis allows the identification of dominant motions and conformational changes by projecting atomic displacements onto principal components.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The input files consist of:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} file containing the projection of atomic displacements onto PC1 and PC2 (typically generated using \sphinxtitleref{gmx covar} and \sphinxtitleref{gmx anaeig})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} file containing the eigenvalues for each principal component (typically \sphinxtitleref{eigenval.xvg} from \sphinxtitleref{gmx anaeig})

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Code Execution}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Import the PCA analysis function:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{dynamispectra}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{PCA}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{pca\PYGZus{}analysis}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\PYG{n}{eigenval\PYGZus{}path} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+s+sa}{r}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{C:}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Users}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Conrado}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Desktop}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{DynamiSpectra}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{data}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{PCA}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{eigenval.xvg}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}

This will generate a PCA scatter plot where each point represents a frame projected in the PC1–PC2 space, colored according to simulation time. The fraction of variance explained by PC1 and PC2 is automatically extracted from the eigenvalue file and included in the axis labels. You can modify the colormap, point size, and transparency as needed for presentation or publication purposes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To use default settings, omit the optional keyword arguments.

\label{\detokenize{Input:secondary-structure-probability}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} provides tools for the analysis and comparison of secondary structure content across different simulation groups. \sphinxAtStartPar
These \sphinxtitleref{.dat} files are typically generated by external tools such as \sphinxstylestrong{dssp} in GROMACS or \sphinxtitleref{gmx dssp}, followed by post\sphinxhyphen{}processing to calculate structure probabilities per residue.

\section{Secondary Structure Fractions}
\label{\detokenize{Input:secondary-structure-fractions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} allows visualization of the time evolution of global secondary structure content during molecular dynamics simulations. This analysis provides insights into the overall structural dynamics by quantifying the fraction of residues adopting each secondary structure type (helix, sheet, coil) per frame.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The input \sphinxtitleref{.dat} file must contain secondary structure assignments per frame, usually obtained using \sphinxtitleref{gmx dssp} followed by conversion to per\sphinxhyphen{}frame structural fractions.

\sphinxstylestrong{Code Execution}

\section{Density Analysis}
\label{\detokenize{Input:density-analysis}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} allows analysis and visualization of system density throughout molecular dynamics simulations. This provides insight into system stability, phase transitions, and equilibration.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This module processes \sphinxtitleref{.xvg} files typically generated by GROMACS during simulation or via energy analysis tools.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To obtain density data from GROMACS, you can use the following command after your simulation:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }energy\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.edr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}o\PYG{+w}{ }density.xvg
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Select the density property when prompted.

\chapter{RMSD}
\label{\detokenize{RMSD:rmsd}}\label{\detokenize{RMSD::doc}}

\section{Overview}
\label{\detokenize{RMSD:overview}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} enables comprehensive analysis of Root Mean Square Deviation (RMSD) from molecular dynamics simulations using .xvg files. The tool supports the processing of multiple replicates per simulation group, allowing the calculation of average and standard deviation to capture structural deviations over time. However, it can also be applied to a single replicate, making it suitable for both exploratory analyses and more robust comparative studies involving multiple trajectories.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The generated plots provide time series visualizations with shaded standard deviations and kernel density distributions of RMSD values. This allows users to assess the dynamic stability of systems across simulations and compare structural drift between conditions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Command line in GROMACS to generate .xvg files for the analysis:}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }rms\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }index.ndx\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}tu\PYG{+w}{ }ns\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}o\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xvg
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{rmsd\PYGZus{}analysis}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{output\PYGZus{}folder}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{simulation\PYGZus{}file\PYGZus{}groups}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{rmsd\PYGZus{}config}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{None}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{density\PYGZus{}config}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{None}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{RMSD}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Interpretation guidence:} This plot illustrates the temporal evolution of structural deviation relative to the reference conformation during the simulation. A stable RMSD plateau indicates that the system has equilibrated and maintains a consistent structure. Gradual increases or large fluctuations suggest ongoing conformational changes, instability, or unfolding events. Assessing the RMSD trend helps identify when the system reaches equilibrium and whether structural deviations remain within expected biological variability.

\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[width=500\sphinxpxdimen]{{RMSD_density}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Interpretation guidence:} This plot shows how frequently different RMSD values occur during the simulation. Sharp peaks indicate stable conformations, while broader or multiple peaks reveal structural flexibility or transitions between states.

\chapter{RMSF}
\label{\detokenize{RMSF:rmsf}}\label{\detokenize{RMSF::doc}}

\section{Overview}
\label{\detokenize{RMSF:overview}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} provides a comprehensive Root Mean Square Fluctuation (RMSF) analysis package for molecular dynamics simulations using .xvg input files. The RMSF module supports analysis of individual simulation replicas and computes averages and standard deviations across multiple replicates. The graphical outputs show the average RMSF with a shaded area representing the standard deviation, facilitating visualization of flexibility patterns.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Command line in GROMACS to generate .xvg files for the analysis:}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }rmsf\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}o\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xvg\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}res
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{rmsf\PYGZus{}analysis}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{output\PYGZus{}folder}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{simulation\PYGZus{}files\PYGZus{}groups}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{rmsf\PYGZus{}config}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{None}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{density\PYGZus{}config}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{None}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{RMSF}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Interpretation guidence:} This graph shows RMSF values across residues, where higher peaks indicate regions of greater flexibility or mobility, such as loops or termini. Lower values correspond to more rigid regions like helices or sheets. Observing these patterns helps identify functionally important flexible segments and assess the dynamic behavior of the system. Comparing RMSF profiles with references helps determine if observed fluctuations are expected or significant.

\chapter{Radius of gyration}
\label{\detokenize{Rg:radius-of-gyration}}\label{\detokenize{Rg::doc}}

\section{Overview}
\label{\detokenize{Rg:overview}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} provides a robust analytical tool for evaluating the radius of gyration (Rg) from molecular dynamics simulations using .xvg input files. This module supports the analysis of individual simulation replicas as well as the computation of average Rg values and standard deviations across replicates. Visual outputs include time series plots with shaded variability and Rg density distributions for each simulation group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This analysis helps monitor the structural compactness and stability of macromolecules over time, offering valuable insight into folding behavior, domain organization, or global conformational changes throughout the simulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Command line in GROMACS to generate .xvg files for the analysis:}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }gyrate\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}o\PYG{+w}{ }gyrate\PYGZus{}simulation.xvg
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{rg\PYGZus{}analysis}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{output\PYGZus{}folder}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{simulation\PYGZus{}groups}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{rg\PYGZus{}config}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{None}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{density\PYGZus{}config}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{None}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{Rg}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{How to interpret}: This plot illustrates the evolution of the radius of gyration over time. A stable or consistent Rg profile indicates that the system maintains a compact and well\sphinxhyphen{}defined structure throughout the simulation. In contrast, marked increases or decreases in Rg may reflect molecular expansion, unfolding, or compaction. Evaluating Rg trends in relation to expected structural behavior helps determine whether the system’s compactness aligns with its functional or biological role.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{plot\PYGZus{}density}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{results}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{output\PYGZus{}folder}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{config}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[width=500\sphinxpxdimen]{{Rg_density}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{How to interpret}: This plot shows the density distribution of the radius of gyration values throughout the simulation. Peaks in the distribution indicate the most frequently sampled Rg values. Sharper, well\sphinxhyphen{}defined peaks suggest structural stability and consistency across time or replicates, while broader peaks reflect greater variability in system compactness.

\chapter{Hydrogen Bond Analysis}
\label{\detokenize{Hbond:hydrogen-bond-analysis}}\label{\detokenize{Hbond::doc}}

\section{Overview}
\label{\detokenize{Hbond:overview}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} provides a comprehensive and versatile analytical framework for quantifying and monitoring hydrogen bond dynamics throughout molecular dynamics simulations. Using input data in standardized .xvg file format, this module enables detailed evaluation of hydrogen bonding interactions that are essential for understanding molecular stability, conformational changes, and interaction patterns.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This analysis offers an in\sphinxhyphen{}depth view of hydrogen bond formation and disruption over time. When multiple simulation replicates are available, \sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} calculates averaged hydrogen bond counts and associated variability measures, such as standard deviation, to provide statistically robust insights. The software also supports analysis of individual replicas, offering flexibility when replicate data is limited or unavailable.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Command line in GROMACS to generate .xvg files for the analysis:}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }hbond\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}num\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xvg\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}tu\PYG{+w}{ }ns
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Note:} The hydrogen bond analysis module in \sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} also supports the analysis of inter\sphinxhyphen{}residue hydrogen bonds within the protein, as well as hydrogen bonds between the protein and ligand. Users simply need to select the appropriate groups during analysis and generate the corresponding .xvg output files.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{hbond\PYGZus{}analysis}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{output\PYGZus{}folder}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{simulation\PYGZus{}file\PYGZus{}groups}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{hbond\PYGZus{}config}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{None}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{density\PYGZus{}config}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{None}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{Hbond}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{How to interpret}: This plot illustrates the temporal evolution of hydrogen bond counts within the system. Stable trends indicate persistent hydrogen bonding and structural integrity, while fluctuations may reflect conformational changes or dynamic instabilities. Comparative analysis across simulations can reveal consistencies or discrepancies attributable to differing initial conditions or simulation parameters. Variations in hydrogen bond numbers over time often correspond to the formation or disruption of critical molecular interactions, providing valuable insight into the system’s behavior.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{plot\PYGZus{}density}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{results}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{output\PYGZus{}folder}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{config}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[width=500\sphinxpxdimen]{{Hbond_density}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{How to interpret}: This plot represents the density distribution of hydrogen bonds observed throughout the simulations. The x\sphinxhyphen{}axis corresponds to the number of hydrogen bonds, while the y\sphinxhyphen{}axis denotes their frequency density. Regions with higher density indicate more frequent occurrences of specific hydrogen bond counts. Comparing density profiles across simulations enables the identification of similarities or divergences in hydrogen bonding patterns, offering valuable insights into the stability and interaction dynamics of the molecular system.

\chapter{Solvent Accessible Surface Area}
\label{\detokenize{SASA:solvent-accessible-surface-area}}\label{\detokenize{SASA::doc}}

\section{Overview}
\label{\detokenize{SASA:overview}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} provides a comprehensive Solvent Accessible Surface Area (SASA) analysis module for molecular dynamics simulations. This module supports both individual replica analysis and the calculation of statistical metrics (mean and standard deviation) across multiple simulation replicas. The resulting plots display the average SASA over time with shaded regions representing the variability across replicates. This enables users to assess trends in solvent exposure and compare results across different conditions or systems.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Command line in GROMACS to generate .xvg files for the analysis:}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }sasa\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}o\PYG{+w}{ }sasa\PYGZus{}simulation.xvg\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}probe\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}.14
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{sasa\PYGZus{}analysis}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{output\PYGZus{}folder}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{simulation\PYGZus{}files\PYGZus{}groups}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{sasa\PYGZus{}config}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{None}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{density\PYGZus{}config}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{None}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{SASA}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Interpretation guidence} This graph shows the SASA over time, with the mean and standard deviation across replicas. A stable SASA indicates that the system maintains a consistent solvent\sphinxhyphen{}exposed surface area. Sudden increases may reflect unfolding or expansion, while decreases can suggest compaction or structural collapse. Monitoring SASA trends helps reveal conformational changes during the simulation.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{plot\PYGZus{}density}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{means\PYGZus{}list}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{output\PYGZus{}folder}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{config}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[width=500\sphinxpxdimen]{{SASA_density}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Interpretation guidence:} This graph shows the probability distribution of SASA values across the simulation. Peaks indicate the most frequently sampled solvent\sphinxhyphen{}accessible areas. Narrow, sharp peaks suggest structural stability, while broader distributions reflect greater conformational variability. Comparing curves across simulations can reveal differences in surface exposure behavior.

    \PYG{k}{return} \PYG{n}{times}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{np}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{mean}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{sasas}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{axis}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{np}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{std}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{sasas}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{axis}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{)}

\chapter{Salt bridge}
\label{\detokenize{Saltbridge:salt-bridge}}\label{\detokenize{Saltbridge::doc}}

\section{Overview}
\label{\detokenize{Saltbridge:overview}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} offers a robust salt bridge analysis tool for molecular dynamics simulations. This module tracks the minimum distances between charged groups in the protein and ligand over time, using input data in standardized .xvg file format. It supports analysis of individual replicas as well as averaging across multiple replicas, providing mean distances and variability (standard deviation). The generated plots visualize the temporal evolution of these distances, with shaded regions indicating the variability, facilitating clear interpretation of salt bridge stability.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Command line in GROMACS to generate .xvg files for the analysis:}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

Comparing distance values with known thresholds or reference data helps determine the significance of the salt bridge throughout the simulation.

\chapter{Protein\sphinxhyphen{}Ligand Contacts}
\label{\detokenize{Contacts:protein-ligand-contacts}}\label{\detokenize{Contacts::doc}}

\section{Overview}
\label{\detokenize{Contacts:overview}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} offers a robust analytical framework to quantify the number of contacts between protein and ligand throughout molecular dynamics simulations, utilizing input data in .xvg file format. This analysis facilitates a detailed characterization of intermolecular interactions and binding dynamics.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The software’s graphical interface enables the visualization of the average number of contacts calculated across multiple simulation replicates, with the associated standard deviation represented as a shaded region illustrating variability. Furthermore, \sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} accommodates the analysis of individual simulation replicas, allowing users to generate plots from a single dataset when multiple replicas are unavailable or unnecessary.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Command line in GROMACS to generate .xvg files for the analysis:}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }mindist\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }index.ndx\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}on\PYG{+w}{ }Contacts.xvg\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}d\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}.35
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{Contacts}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Interpretation guidance:} The resulting plots depict the temporal evolution of protein\sphinxhyphen{}ligand contacts. A stable profile suggests persistent interactions and binding stability, whereas notable deviations may indicate conformational changes, ligand dissociation events, or alternative binding modes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Interpretation guidance:} This plot depicts the density distribution derived from the temporal profile of protein\sphinxhyphen{}ligand contacts. Peaks in the distribution correspond to regions exhibiting a higher frequency of interactions. Broader peaks indicate a more heterogeneous or variable contact pattern, while sharper, more pronounced peaks reflect stable and well\sphinxhyphen{}defined interaction regions between the protein and ligand.

\chapter{Protein\sphinxhyphen{}Ligand Minimal Distance}
\label{\detokenize{Distance:protein-ligand-minimal-distance}}\label{\detokenize{Distance::doc}}

\section{Overview}
\label{\detokenize{Distance:overview}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} provides a rigorous and versatile analytical framework designed to quantify and monitor the dynamic distances between protein and ligand molecules throughout the course of molecular dynamics simulations. Utilizing input data in standardized .xvg file format, this module enables researchers to precisely evaluate intermolecular spatial relationships, which are critical for understanding binding affinity, conformational changes, and interaction stability.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This analysis offers a comprehensive perspective on how the proximity between the protein and ligand evolves over time, allowing identification of transient interactions, stable binding modes, or dissociation events. By incorporating multiple simulation replicates, \sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} calculates averaged distance profiles along with corresponding measures of variability, such as standard deviation, to provide statistically meaningful insights. Additionally, the software accommodates the evaluation of individual simulation replicas, enabling flexible application where replicate data may be limited or unnecessary.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Command line in GROMACS to generate .xvg files for the analysis:}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }mindist\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }index.ndx\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}od\PYG{+w}{ }Distance.xvg\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}d\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}.35
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{Distance}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Interpretation guidance:} The resulting plots depict the temporal evolution of the minimal distances between protein and ligand atoms. Consistently low minimal distances suggest stable close contacts or binding, while significant increases or fluctuations may indicate conformational changes, ligand dissociation, or transient interactions

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[width=500\sphinxpxdimen]{{distance_density}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Interpretation guidance:} This plot illustrates the density distribution derived from the temporal profile of the minimal distance between protein and ligand. Peaks in the distribution signify regions where the minimal distances occur more frequently, indicating preferred interaction distances. Broader peaks suggest a more variable and heterogeneous range of distances, while sharper, well\sphinxhyphen{}defined peaks reflect stable and consistent interaction proximities throughout the simulation.

\chapter{Protein–Ligand Hydrophobic Contacts}
\label{\detokenize{Hydrophobic_contacts:proteinligand-hydrophobic-contacts}}\label{\detokenize{Hydrophobic_contacts::doc}}

\section{Overview}
\label{\detokenize{Hydrophobic_contacts:overview}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} offers a robust and versatile analytical framework designed to quantify and monitor hydrophobic contacts between protein and ligand molecules throughout molecular dynamics simulations. Utilizing input data in standardized .xvg file format, this module enables researchers to characterize the extent and dynamics of hydrophobic interactions, which are fundamental for molecular recognition, binding affinity, and complex stability.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This analysis provides detailed insights into the temporal evolution of hydrophobic contacts, allowing identification of transient contacts, persistent hydrophobic patches, or disruption of interactions. By incorporating data from multiple simulation replicates, \sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} computes averaged contact profiles with corresponding variability measures, such as standard deviation, facilitating statistically meaningful interpretation. Moreover, the software supports analysis of individual simulation replicas, enabling flexible usage when replicate data are unavailable or unnecessary.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Command line in GROMACS to generate .xvg files for the analysis:}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{select}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }index.ndx\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}select\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}group \PYGZdq{}LIG\PYGZdq{} and within 0.6 of (resname ALA VAL LEU ILE PHE MET and group \PYGZdq{}Protein\PYGZdq{})\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}os\PYG{+w}{ }Hydrophobic\PYGZus{}contacts.xvg
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{hydrophobic\PYGZus{}analysis}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{output\PYGZus{}folder}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{simulation\PYGZus{}file\PYGZus{}groups}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{contact\PYGZus{}config}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{None}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{density\PYGZus{}config}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{None}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{Hydrophobic_contacts}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Interpretation guidance:} The resulting plots illustrate the temporal progression of hydrophobic contacts between protein and ligand. A consistently high number of contacts indicates stable hydrophobic interactions and sustained binding affinity, whereas notable decreases or fluctuations may reflect conformational changes, disruption of hydrophobic patches, or transient binding events.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{plot\PYGZus{}contact\PYGZus{}density}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{results}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{output\PYGZus{}folder}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{config}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{None}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[width=500\sphinxpxdimen]{{Hydrophobic_contacts_density}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Interpretation guidance:} This plot represents the density distribution derived from the temporal profile of minimal distances between protein and ligand. Peaks in the distribution indicate preferred interaction distances that occur more frequently during the simulation. Broader peaks suggest a more heterogeneous and variable range of distances, whereas sharper and well\sphinxhyphen{}defined peaks reflect stable and consistent spatial proximities maintained throughout the simulation.

\chapter{Inter\sphinxhyphen{}residue Distance Matrix}
\label{\detokenize{DistanceMatrix:inter-residue-distance-matrix}}\label{\detokenize{DistanceMatrix::doc}}

\section{Overview}
\label{\detokenize{DistanceMatrix:overview}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} provides a detailed analytical tool to calculate and visualize inter\sphinxhyphen{}residue distance matrices within molecular systems during molecular dynamics simulations, using input data in .xpm file formats. This analysis allows researchers to examine the spatial relationships and dynamic proximities between residues of a single molecular entity, such as a protein, thereby offering insights into structural conformations and intra\sphinxhyphen{}molecular interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The inter\sphinxhyphen{}residue distance matrix represents pairwise distances between residues across the entire molecular chain, enabling the identification of stable contacts, flexible regions, and conformational rearrangements.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Command line in GROMACS to generate .xvg files for the analysis:}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }mdmat\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}mean\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xpm\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}no\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xvg
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{distance\PYGZus{}matrix\PYGZus{}analysis}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{xpm\PYGZus{}file\PYGZus{}path}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{output\PYGZus{}path}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{None}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{plot}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{True}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{config}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{None}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{DistanceMatrix}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Interpretation guidance:} The resulting distance matrix is represented as a colored map, where darker regions correspond to larger inter\sphinxhyphen{}residue distances and lighter regions indicate closer proximities. This visualization enables the identification of tightly packed or interacting residue pairs as lighter areas, while more distant residues appear as darker zones.

\chapter{Phi and Psi Angles}
\label{\detokenize{PhiPsi:phi-and-psi-angles}}\label{\detokenize{PhiPsi::doc}}

\section{Overview}
\label{\detokenize{PhiPsi:overview}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} provides a robust and flexible analytical framework for analyzing backbone dihedral angles φ (phi) and ψ (psi) of proteins throughout molecular dynamics simulations. Utilizing .xvg files generated from simulation outputs, this module enables detailed assessment of protein conformational preferences and structural dynamics by capturing the distribution and evolution of φ and ψ angles over time.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This analysis offers comprehensive insights into predominant conformations, conformational transitions, and rare structural states. The graphical outputs generated by \sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} facilitate clear visualization of protein backbone angular patterns, supporting both qualitative and quantitative interpretation of protein structural dynamics.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Command line in GROMACS to generate .xvg files for the analysis:}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }rama\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}o\PYG{+w}{ }rama\PYGZus{}simulation.xvg
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Note:} \sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} generates individual phi and psi density plots for each simulation replica, as well as a combined density plot using data concatenated from all replicas. The concatenated density plot provides a comprehensive overview of the conformational space sampled across simulations, enabling identification of predominant structural states and improving statistical robustness compared to analyzing replicas separately.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{phipsi\PYGZus{}analysis}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{output\PYGZus{}folder}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{simulation\PYGZus{}file\PYGZus{}groups}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{phipsi\PYGZus{}config}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{None}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{residue\PYGZus{}name}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{None}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[width=600\sphinxpxdimen]{{PhiPsi}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Interpretation guidance:} This plot presents a color density map of the sampled backbone dihedral angles (phi and psi) of the protein or residue throughout the molecular dynamics simulation. Regions with stronger (more intense) colors indicate higher density, meaning the protein or residue spent more time adopting those angular conformations, reflecting preferred and stable states. Conversely, areas with weaker colors represent lower density regions with less frequent or transient conformations. This visualization provides valuable insights into the conformational flexibility and dynamic behavior of the protein during the simulation.


\section{Complete code}
\label{\detokenize{PhiPsi:complete-code}}

\chapter{Rotamers}
\label{\detokenize{Rotamers:rotamers}}\label{\detokenize{Rotamers::doc}}

\section{Overview}
\label{\detokenize{Rotamers:overview}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} provides a comprehensive framework for analyzing protein side chain rotameric states by examining the Chi1 and Chi2 dihedral angles during molecular dynamics simulations. Using input .xvg files, this module calculates circular means of these angles across multiple simulation replicas, allowing robust statistical analysis of side chain conformational dynamics.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The module generates three types of plots: a 2D kernel density estimate (KDE) to visualize preferred rotamer conformations, a dotplot showing mean Chi1 versus Chi2 angles over time, and histograms displaying the distribution of individual Chi1 and Chi2 angles. This enables detailed characterization of rotamer populations, transitions, and conformational preferences critical for understanding protein function and dynamics.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Command line in GROMACS to generate .xvg files for the analysis:}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }angle\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }index.ndx\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}type\PYG{+w}{ }dihedral\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}ov\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xvg
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Note:} The atoms that define the Chi1 and Chi2 dihedral angles must be specified in the index file (.ndx) used with the gmx angle command. Ensure that the correct atom quadruplets are selected for each angle to obtain accurate rotameric data.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{dihedral\PYGZus{}kde\PYGZus{}and\PYGZus{}dotplot}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{output\PYGZus{}folder}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{chi1\PYGZus{}files}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{chi2\PYGZus{}files}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{config}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{None}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{time\PYGZus{}window}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{None}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[width=600\sphinxpxdimen]{{Kde2d}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Interpretation guidence:} This 2D kernel density estimate (KDE) plot shows the distribution of Chi1 and Chi2 side\sphinxhyphen{}chain dihedral angles over the simulation. Darker regions correspond to higher estimated densities, indicating that those angular combinations were more frequently sampled. These high\sphinxhyphen{}density zones reveal preferred rotameric states adopted by the residue, while lighter areas indicate less frequent conformations. This plot provides insight into side\sphinxhyphen{}chain conformational preferences and flexibility during the simulation.

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[width=600\sphinxpxdimen]{{dotplot}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Interpretation guidence:} This plot displays the mean Chi1 and Chi2 dihedral angles over the course of the simulation or within a defined time window. Each point represents the averaged side chain conformation across multiple replicas at a given time. Clusters or patterns in the plot indicate preferred rotameric states, while dispersion suggests conformational variability. This visualization is useful for identifying dominant side chain orientations and assessing the dynamic range of rotameric transitions within the selected period.

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[width=600\sphinxpxdimen]{{histogram}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Interpretation guidence:} This histogram depicts the distribution density of dihedral angles observed during the simulation or within a selected time window. Distinct peaks indicate preferred rotamer conformations, while broader or multiple peaks suggest increased conformational flexibility or transitions between states.

\chapter{Ligand Density}
\label{\detokenize{Ligand Density:ligand-density}}\label{\detokenize{Ligand Density::doc}}

\section{Overview}
\label{\detokenize{Ligand Density:overview}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} provides a comprehensive and versatile analytical framework designed to quantify and monitor the spatial density distribution of ligand molecules within molecular dynamics simulations. Utilizing input data in standardized .xpm file format, this module enables researchers to characterize ligand localization, aggregation, and dynamic behavior within the simulated environment.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This analysis offers detailed insights into the spatial distribution of ligand density, facilitating the identification of preferential binding regions, ligand clustering, or dispersal events. The graphical outputs generated by \sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} enable straightforward visualization of ligand density patterns throughout the simulation, supporting qualitative and quantitative interpretation of ligand behavior.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Command line in GROMACS to generate .xvg files for the analysis:}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }densmap\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }index.ndx\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}o\PYG{+w}{ }map.xpm\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}aver\PYG{+w}{ }z
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Explanation of Axes:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The generated density map is a 2D projection of ligand atomic positions onto the XY plane of the simulation box. This projection is done by averaging coordinates along the Z\sphinxhyphen{}axis over the trajectory frames.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{X axis:} corresponds to the simulation box’s X spatial coordinate (in nanometers)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Y axis:} corresponds to the simulation box’s Y spatial coordinate (in nanometers)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This means that the labels “X” and “Y” on the plot directly represent physical coordinates in real space, consistent with the standard Cartesian coordinate system used in molecular dynamics.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{ligand\PYGZus{}density\PYGZus{}analysis}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{xpm\PYGZus{}file\PYGZus{}path}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{output\PYGZus{}path}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{None}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{plot}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{True}\PYG{p}{,}
                        \PYG{n}{cmap}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{inferno}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{xlabel}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{X}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{ylabel}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Y}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
                        \PYG{n}{title}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{colorbar\PYGZus{}label}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Relative density}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
                        \PYG{n}{figsize}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{6}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{5}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{label\PYGZus{}fontsize}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mi}{12}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[width=600\sphinxpxdimen]{{ligand_density}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Interpretation guidance:} This plot illustrates the relative density distribution of ligand atoms throughout the simulation. Regions with higher density values correspond to areas where the ligand spent more time, indicating preferred binding locations or stable interaction zones. Conversely, areas with lower density indicate less frequent ligand presence or greater positional variability.

\chapter{Ligand Angle}
\label{\detokenize{Ligand angle:ligand-angle}}\label{\detokenize{Ligand angle::doc}}

\section{Overview}
\label{\detokenize{Ligand angle:overview}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} provides a comprehensive and versatile analytical framework designed to quantify and monitor the spatial distribution and dynamics of ligand angular conformations throughout molecular dynamics simulations. Utilizing input data in standardized .xvg file format, this module enables researchers to characterize ligand conformational preferences, rotational flexibility, and dynamic behavior within the simulated environment.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This analysis delivers detailed insights into the distribution and evolution of ligand angles, facilitating identification of predominant conformations, conformational transitions, or rare states. The graphical outputs generated by \sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} support clear visualization of ligand angular patterns over time, enabling both qualitative and quantitative interpretation of ligand structural dynamics.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Command line in GROMACS to generate .xvg files for the analysis:}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }angle\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.ndx\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}type\PYG{+w}{ }dihedral\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}od\PYG{+w}{ }diedro\PYGZus{}ligand.xvg
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Note:} The .ndx file must include a group containing the specific atoms that define the dihedral angle of interest for the ligand. Proper selection of these atoms is essential for accurate calculation and analysis of ligand dihedral angles.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{angle\PYGZus{}ligand\PYGZus{}analysis}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{output\PYGZus{}folder}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{simulation\PYGZus{}groups}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{time\PYGZus{}config}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{None}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{density\PYGZus{}config}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{None}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{kde2d\PYGZus{}config}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{None}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{ligand_angle_time}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Interpretation guidance:} This plot shows the temporal evolution of the ligand’s dihedral angle across simulations. The consistent range and overlapping curves suggest similar torsional behavior. Fluctuations indicate dynamic flexibility within the sampled timescale.

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{ligand_angle_kde2d}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Interpretation guidance:} This 2D KDE plot represents the temporal evolution of the ligand’s dihedral angle, computed as the circular mean across all replicas within each simulation group. If a simulation includes six replicas, their angular profiles are combined through circular averaging to generate a single, smoothed density map. The result reveals dominant conformational states and transitions over time, highlighting regions of stability and fluctuation.

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[width=500\sphinxpxdimen]{{ligand_angle_density}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Interpretation guidance:} The density plot compares the overall distribution of dihedral angles across simulations. A narrow peak suggests rigidity, while broader or multiple peaks indicate flexible or metastable conformations. Differences between curves reflect variability across replicates.

\chapter{Principal Component Analysis}
\label{\detokenize{PCA:principal-component-analysis}}\label{\detokenize{PCA::doc}}

\section{Overview}
\label{\detokenize{PCA:overview}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{DynamiSpectra} offers a robust and versatile analytical framework for performing principal component analysis (PCA) on molecular dynamics simulation data. Utilizing input in standardized .xvg file format, this module enables researchers to identify and characterize the dominant collective motions and conformational fluctuations of biomolecular systems.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Command line in GROMACS to generate .xvg files for the analysis:}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }covar\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}o\PYG{+w}{ }eingenvalues.xvg\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}v\PYG{+w}{ }eingenvectors.trr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}av\PYG{+w}{ }average.pdb
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gmx\PYG{+w}{ }anaeig\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}v\PYG{+w}{ }eingenvectors.trr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.xtc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }Simulation.tpr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}first\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}last\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}2d\PYG{+w}{ }2dproj.xvg
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Note:} PCA analysis requires the eigenvalues.xvg and 2dproj.xvg files.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{pca\PYGZus{}analysis}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{pca\PYGZus{}file\PYGZus{}path}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{eigenval\PYGZus{}path}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{output\PYGZus{}folder}\PYG{p}{,}
             \PYG{n}{title}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{PCA}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{figsize}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{7}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{6}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{cmap}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{viridis}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
             \PYG{n}{point\PYGZus{}size}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mi}{30}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{alpha}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.8}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[width=600\sphinxpxdimen]{{PCA}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{How to interpret:} This plot illustrates the temporal or spatial distribution of motion projected along selected principal components (PCs). The first few PCs generally capture the most significant large\sphinxhyphen{}scale motions within the system. Dense clustering of data points may indicate stable conformational states, whereas more dispersed distributions suggest increased structural variability or transitions between different dynamic regimes.
